main_damage_causes: Loss of Hagrid's personal grief and emotional depth in multiple intimate scenes (baby Harry farewell, Voldemort story, hospital wing remorse), reducing him from a man with a deep personal stake in Harry's story to a warm but functionally driven guide

Removal of the Underground/train journey (cut scene) eliminates both his comic fish-out-of-water Muggle-world characterisation and the foundational plant for his dragon obsession, weakening the Norbert subplot's characterological grounding

Compression of Hagrid's moral voice — his defence of Muggle-born witches, his Slytherin warning, his empathy for Quirrell — means the film Hagrid is less fully established as an active ethical presence with convictions, relying almost entirely on warmth and loyalty rather than a rounded moral personality
Compression of Hagrid's extended cabin scenes removes his wit, perceptiveness, humor, and mischief, flattening him from a multi-layered presence into a warm but one-dimensional supporting figure

Reduction of physical agency in confrontation scenes (Flourish and Blotts brawl, end-feast reunion) replaces Hagrid's characteristically embodied emotional expression with more passive or conventionally sentimental alternatives

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Hut-on-the-Rock arrival — Hagrid's emotional farewell to baby Harry omitted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Hagrid's deep personal grief at leaving Harry: he asks to say goodbye, bends his great shaggy head to give Harry a scratchy whiskery kiss, then lets out a howl like a wounded dog, sobs that he can't stand it — 'Lily an' James dead — an' poor little Harry off ter live with Muggles.' He weeps openly, burying his face in a spotted handkerchief, shoulders shaking, wiping streaming eyes on his jacket sleeve. This is the first major revelation of Hagrid's emotional depth and his personal bond with the Potters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hagrid sniffles and clears his throat as he hands the baby to Dumbledore, but there is no goodbye kiss, no howl, no named grief over Lily and James, no spotted handkerchief, and no sobbing dialogue. The moment is brief and largely silent. Hagrid is a delivery mechanism rather than a grieving man.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's opening Hagrid scene establishes from page one that he is a man of enormous, uninhibited emotion who loved the Potters personally. The film strips this to a functional transaction. The audience loses the immediate understanding that Hagrid's loyalty to Harry is rooted in love and grief, not merely duty.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Hut-on-the-Rock — Hagrid's active, wrathful defence of Harry's identity removed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book shows Hagrid progressively escalating in fury at the Dursleys: he thunders 'ALL WHAT?', leaps to his feet filling the whole hut, growls at the Dursleys demanding to know if Harry knows 'nothin' abou' — about ANYTHING', booms 'DURSLEY!', and then, when Vernon insults Dumbledore, seizes his umbrella, whirls it overhead, and thunders 'NEVER — INSULT — ALBUS — DUMBLEDORE — IN — FRONT — OF — ME!' He also directly confronts the lie about the car crash with 'CAR CRASH! How could a car crash kill Lily an' James Potter? It's an outrage! A scandal!' and defends Harry's right to attend Hogwarts at length. Throughout he demonstrates fierce moral indignation on Harry's behalf.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hagrid's anger at the Dursleys is compressed. He says 'Dry up, Dursley, you great prune', reacts to the car crash revelation with 'A car crash? A car crash killed Lily and James Potter?! 'S an outrage! 'S a scandal!' and defends Hogwarts briefly. The sustained escalating rage — the leaping to his feet, the multiple thunderous outbursts, the full 'NEVER INSULT ALBUS DUMBLEDORE' speech during which he whirls the umbrella — is condensed. The pigtail hex on Dudley is retained.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to establish that Hagrid's warmth has a fierce counterpart: righteous, volcanic anger when people he loves are wronged. The film retains traces but loses the full arc of escalation that makes Hagrid's protective fury a defining character trait.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Hut-on-the-Rock — Hagrid's self-aware rueful humour after the pigtail hex
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After hexing Dudley, book-Hagrid looks down at his umbrella, strokes his beard, and says ruefully: 'Shouldn'ta lost me temper — but it didn't work anyway. Meant ter turn him into a pig, but I suppose he was so much like a pig anyway there wasn't much left ter do.' He then immediately asks Harry not to mention it at Hogwarts, explaining that he is not supposed to do magic, was expelled in his third year, and his wand was snapped. This passage shows Hagrid's self-deprecating wit, his self-awareness about his own rules-violations, and delivers the important backstory about his expulsion.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hagrid simply says 'I'd appreciate it if yeh didn't tell anyone at Hogwarts about tha'. Strictly speakin', I'm not allowed ter do magic.' The rueful pig joke is absent. There is no explanation of the expulsion or the snapped wand in this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The pig joke is a small but telling moment of Hagrid's dry, self-aware humour and his capacity to laugh at himself. Its loss, combined with the absence of the expulsion backstory here, slightly flattens his characterisation in his first major scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Journey to Diagon Alley — Hagrid's Underground/train behaviour and dragon enthusiasm cut (excluded scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes during the journey that Hagrid got stuck in the ticket barrier on the Underground, complained loudly that seats were too small and trains too slow, said 'I don't know how the Muggles manage without magic', took up two seats on the train, and knitted what looked like a canary-yellow circus tent — all of which build his comic fish-out-of-water personality in the Muggle world. He also openly tells Harry 'Crikey, I'd like a dragon. Wanted one ever since I was a kid' when Harry asks about Gringotts' dragons, establishing this desire as a long-standing character trait before it becomes plot-relevant.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Underground journey scene was cut from the theatrical release per the non-theatrical exclusion note. The dragon-wanting admission ('Crikey, I'd like a dragon. Wanted one ever since I was a kid') consequently rests only on the cut scene and is absent from the film. The film has Hagrid state 'Gringotts — t'ain no safer place' but the comic Muggle-world behaviour and the dragon longing disclosure are both lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The cut removes two things: (1) a rich vein of physical comedy that defines Hagrid's relationship with the Muggle world, and (2) the plant for Hagrid's dragon obsession that makes the Norbert subplot feel characterologically motivated rather than arbitrary. Later in the film, Ron has to supply the dragon-wanting information ('Hagrid always wanted a dragon, he told me so the first time I ever met him'), but that rests on a moment the film audience never witnessed, creating a slight credibility gap.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Leaky Cauldron — Hagrid's explanation of Quirrell's backstory omitted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after the Leaky Cauldron celebrity encounter, Hagrid explains unprompted: 'Poor bloke. Brilliant mind. He was fine while he was studyin' outta books but then he took a year off ter get some firsthand experience... They say he met vampires in the Black Forest, and there was a nasty bit o' trouble with a hag — never been the same since. Scared of the students, scared of his own subject now.' This characterises Hagrid as knowledgeable about the wizarding world and generously empathetic toward a flawed colleague.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Hagrid introduce Quirrell briefly ('This is Professor Quirrell. He'll be yer Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher at Hogwarts') and nothing more. No backstory, no empathetic explanation. The warmth and knowledge Hagrid shows in the book scene is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss, but it removes a small demonstration of Hagrid's warmth toward the marginalised and his depth of knowledge about the wizarding world beyond Hogwarts.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Diagon Alley — Hagrid's response to Malfoy boy's 'servant' comment and defence of Muggle-born wizards cut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Harry return to Hagrid after meeting Malfoy in Madam Malkin's and tell him the pale boy said people from Muggle families shouldn't be allowed in. Hagrid responds with warm conviction: 'Yer not from a Muggle family... some o' the best I ever saw were the only ones with magic in 'em in a long line o' Muggles — look at yer mum! Look what she had fer a sister!' This is Hagrid actively countering prejudice and validating Muggle-born witches and wizards with personal testimony.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does not include the visit to Madam Malkin's or the subsequent conversation about blood prejudice with Hagrid. The Malfoy encounter in the robe shop and Hagrid's rebuttal are both absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book moment shows Hagrid as an active advocate against wizarding prejudice who uses Lily Potter as a personal example. Its absence means the film Hagrid never explicitly voices the anti-blood-purity position that is one of his moral defining traits.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Diagon Alley — Hagrid's Slytherin warning and moral clarity cut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Hagrid tell Harry: 'Better Hufflepuff than Slytherin. There's not a single witch or wizard who went bad who wasn't in Slytherin. You-Know-Who was one.' This is a clear moral declaration that establishes Hagrid's uncomplicated ethical worldview and seeds the Slytherin theme early.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This exchange does not appear in the film corpus. Hagrid does not make any statement about Slytherin to Harry during the Diagon Alley visit.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Small loss, but Hagrid's blunt moral categorisation of Slytherin is part of his characterisation as a man of simple but firm ethical convictions. Its absence means the film Hagrid is slightly less defined as a moral voice.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Voldemort backstory scene — relocated from journey context to Leaky Cauldron, structural framing changed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, the Voldemort story is told in the hut at night, during a scene dominated by warmth, sausages, and the aftermath of Hagrid's dramatic arrival — an intimate, private setting. The scene includes Hagrid's reluctance to say the name, his admission he can't spell it, his emotional detour about knowing Lily and James personally ('knew yer mum an' dad, an' nicer people yeh couldn't find'), his pulling out a spotted handkerchief when he mentions their death, and Hagrid's defence of Harry against Vernon's insults by drawing his umbrella. Crucially, Hagrid also says he never expected to have to tell Harry this and questions whether he is 'the right person' to do so, showing self-doubt.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, the Voldemort backstory is told in the Leaky Cauldron over soup, framed as Harry proactively pressing Hagrid ('He killed my parents, didn't he? You know, Hagrid. I know you do.'). Hagrid's personal grief about knowing the Potters is reduced to the narrated flashback. The self-doubt ('I don' know if I'm the right person ter tell yeh') is absent. The scene is shorter and more efficiently functional.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Relocating and compressing the scene loses Hagrid's personal testimony of grief about the Potters and his self-doubt about his fitness to deliver this revelation. These details make book-Hagrid feel like a man with a personal stake in Harry's story rather than an exposition delivery system. The film version is adequate but shallower.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / First tea at Hagrid's — Hagrid's evasion about Snape and his knowledge of the situation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Harry tell Hagrid about Snape's lesson and Hagrid tell him not to worry, that Snape likes hardly any students. But crucially: 'Harry couldn't help thinking that Hagrid didn't quite meet his eyes when he said that.' Then Hagrid abruptly changes the subject to Charlie Weasley. This detail — that Hagrid is actively withholding something he knows about Snape — establishes him as a character with hidden knowledge who is complicit in keeping secrets from Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The tea visit scene is not present in the film corpus. Hagrid's evasive body language about Snape during a private chat with Harry is entirely absent from the film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss, but the book detail of Hagrid not meeting Harry's eyes is a quiet piece of characterisation showing that Hagrid carries the weight of things he cannot say. Its absence contributes to a slightly less layered film Hagrid.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Post-Quidditch discussion — Hagrid dismisses Snape curse theory too flatly, loses dramatic irony nuance
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid says 'Rubbish! Why should he?' and 'Snape's a Hogwarts teacher, he'd do nothin' of the sort' — but this comes after he also 'hadn't heard a word of what had gone on next to him in the stands' and the narrative notes Harry felt Hagrid 'didn't quite meet his eyes' at tea. The accumulated pattern makes clear Hagrid is protecting a secret he knows.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film Hagrid plays these scenes adequately, but without the accumulation of prior evasive signals, his defences of Snape read as simple-minded rather than protectively knowing.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Small reduction in the layered quality of Hagrid's characterisation as someone caught between loyalty to Dumbledore and inadvertent endangerment of Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: PS / Hospital wing ending — Hagrid's remorse scene significantly compressed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Hagrid arrive at the hospital wing, sit next to Harry, and burst into tears: 'It's — all — my — ruddy — fault! I told the evil git how ter get past Fluffy! I told him! It was the only thing he didn't know, an' I told him! Yeh could've died! All fer a dragon egg! I'll never drink again! I should be chucked out an' made ter live as a Muggle!' He then gives Harry the photo album he has assembled by writing to all his parents' school friends. Harry has to comfort Hagrid and shouts 'VOLDEMORT!' to shock him out of crying. The scene is a full emotional beat of guilt, remorse, and gift-giving.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hagrid visits Harry in the hospital wing and simply hands him the photo album: 'This is fer you.' Harry thanks him, shakes his hand, and hugs him. There is no extended remorse speech, no self-flagellation, no 'I'll never drink again', and no Harry comforting Hagrid. The scene is warm but minimal.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene closes Hagrid's arc for the first story by showing him take full moral responsibility for his mistake — a crucial beat in a character whose tragic flaw is that his innocent enthusiasms can cause harm. The film replaces this with a purely tender farewell gift, losing the accountability and the reversal where Harry must comfort the adult. This diminishes the emotional and moral weight of Hagrid's role in the climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Flourish and Blotts bookshop confrontation (Film Scene 1, scene 30)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Hagrid physically separating Mr. Weasley and Lucius Malfoy after a genuine brawl breaks out ('Hagrid was wading toward them through the sea of books... had pulled Mr. Weasley and Mr. Malfoy apart. Mr. Weasley had a cut lip...'). After separating them, Hagrid delivers his moral verdict forcefully ('Yeh should've ignored him, Arthur... Rotten ter the core, the whole family... no Malfoy's worth listenin' ter - bad blood, that's what it is'). This is a full scene with physical action and moral authority.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, there is no actual brawl. Hagrid merely steps forward and puts 'a firm hand on Mr. Weasley's shoulder' before any fight occurs, then delivers a truncated version of his verdict ('Ignore 'im, Arthur' and 'No Malfoy's worth listenin' ter. Rotten ter the core, the whole family...'). Hagrid functions as a passive restraining force rather than a responsive, physically engaged character who then takes moral stock of the situation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book positions Hagrid as someone who acts decisively in a moment of conflict and then takes ownership of the moral lesson. The film reduces him to a bystander who prevents the conflict from even beginning. The loss of the brawl also removes context that shows Hagrid's sheer physical presence as something meaningful in the world — people act differently around him. The moral speech is retained but loses weight because it follows prevention rather than resolution.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Hagrid's hut, slug-vomiting visit (Film Scene 2, scene 46)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book visit to Hagrid's cabin is a rich, extended scene covering: Hagrid's grumpy reception that brightens on seeing them; his practical care for Ron; his pointed commentary on Lockhart ('If one word of it was true, I'll eat my kettle'); his defense of Hermione against the Mudblood slur and pride in her ('they haven't invented a spell our Hermione can't do'); his analysis of the Dark Arts job being jinxed; his teasing of Harry about signed photos and Ginny's crush; his secret use of magic on the pumpkins; and the pumpkin patch tour. Hagrid is warm, funny, wise about the wizarding world, and emotionally perceptive.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film scene (scene 46) is significantly compressed. Hagrid provides the bucket for Ron, explains the Mudblood slur, defends Hermione, and offers some general comfort. The Lockhart criticism, the joke about signed photos, the pumpkin patch with secret Engorgement Charm, the insight about the jinxed DADA position, and Ginny's crush teasing are all absent. The scene functions primarily as an expository vehicle for explaining 'Mudblood' rather than as a character showcase.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene does substantial character work: it shows Hagrid's wit (the signed photo joke), his shrewdness (seeing through Lockhart), his warmth and pride in his students, his mischievous relationship with rules (the Engorgement Charm), and his perceptive teasing (Ginny's crush). The film reduces him to a sympathetic explainer. The cumulative loss of these personality layers meaningfully flattens how the audience perceives Hagrid as a rounded, humorous, emotionally intelligent figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Corridor encounter after diary vision (Film Scene 2, scene 74 — cut scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 94-104 establishes a brief but important corridor encounter: Harry literally walks into Hagrid (bumping into him), Hagrid holds up a dead rooster and explains it is the second one killed this term (foxes or a Blood-Sucking Bugbear), and he notices Harry looks 'hot and bothered,' showing attentive concern. This mirrors the book's pattern of Hagrid being present and perceptive throughout the year's crisis.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Per the non-theatrical material exclusion note, this scene — where Harry meets Hagrid carrying a rooster right after the diary vision — was cut from the theatrical release. The film therefore loses this beat entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The cut is minor in isolation but removes one of the recurring book touchpoints where Hagrid is woven into the texture of the school year — present, noticing, caring. Each such removal incrementally reduces Hagrid's presence and attentiveness in the adaptation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Hagrid's hut, Dumbledore/Fudge/Malfoy scene (Film Scene 3, scene 114)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene (scenes 162-192) has Hagrid showing visible fear and emotional vulnerability ('gone pale and sweaty'), genuine outrage at Malfoy ('leapt to his feet, his shaggy black head grazing the ceiling'), trembling when told he is being taken to Azkaban, and finally a moment of meaningful agency: his coded message ('If yeh ever wanted ter find out some stuff, all they'd have ter do is follow the spiders. That'd lead 'em right! That's all I'm sayin'') is delivered under duress as his parting act — a deliberate choice to help Harry even while being arrested.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the core of this scene faithfully, including Hagrid's coded spider clue, his emotional reactions, his defense of Dumbledore, and his accusation that Malfoy threatened the governors. The adaptation is substantially faithful here.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film handles this scene with reasonable fidelity. Minor compression occurs but the essential character moments — vulnerability, courage, the deliberate spider clue as an act of agency under arrest — are preserved. The damage here is minimal and confidence in scoring this as a significant divergence is low.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Tom Riddle refers to Hagrid as 'that brainless oaf' (Film Scene 3, scene 133)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Tom Riddle refers to Hagrid as 'that great oaf' and later elaborates with contemptuous detail: 'big, blundering Hagrid, in trouble every other week, trying to raise werewolf cubs under his bed, sneaking off to the Forbidden Forest to wrestle trolls.' Riddle also says 'I thought someone must realize that Hagrid couldn't possibly be the Heir of Slytherin... as though Hagrid had the brains, or the power!' The book's Riddle speech provides full context for how Hagrid was framed and why it worked, which implicitly dignifies Hagrid by revealing the injustice clearly.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film (scene 133), Riddle calls Hagrid 'that brainless oaf' and says 'It was my word against Hagrid's. Only Dumbledore seemed to think Hagrid was innocent.' The extended book passage explaining Riddle's contempt and the mechanics of the frame-up is compressed. The film omits the detail about Hagrid's specific misadventures (werewolf cubs, wrestling trolls) that Riddle weaponized, and omits Riddle's explicit acknowledgment that he was surprised the plan worked — which in the book serves to highlight how unjust the system was toward Hagrid.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Riddle monologue does double duty: it reveals Riddle's villainy and simultaneously rehabilitates Hagrid's reputation by showing the audience exactly how he was wronged. The film's compression loses the specificity that makes the injustice vivid and removes the implicit argument that Hagrid's eccentricities were weaponized against him by a manipulative system.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - End feast, Hagrid's return (Film Scene 3, scene 137)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's end-of-year feast has Hagrid arriving and 'cuffing Harry and Ron so hard on the shoulders that they were knocked into their plates of trifle' — a physical, exuberant, characteristically Hagrid gesture of affection and relief. It is brief but tonally perfect: Hagrid expresses emotion through overwhelming physicality rather than words.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film (scene 137), Hagrid arrives to a silent room, looks nervous and embarrassed, then delivers a heartfelt speech ('I jus' want to say... Thanks') to Harry, Ron and Hermione. Harry responds 'There's no Hogwarts without you, Hagrid.' It is a more conventionally emotional, verbal scene. The physical comedy and the characteristically Hagrid mode of expressing emotion through unintentional force is replaced by a sentimental dialogue exchange.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book moment is a perfect distillation of Hagrid's character: his love is so overwhelming it is physically dangerous. The film replaces this with a tender verbal exchange that, while moving, is more generic. The line 'There's no Hogwarts without you, Hagrid' is not in the book and sentimentalizes the reunion in a way that substitutes conventional emotional beats for Hagrid's distinctive idiom. The damage is real but contained — it affects tone and voice more than arc or function.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock/Hippogriff lesson) — Hagrid lifts Harry and drops him onto Buckbeak without preparation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 68-70: Hagrid instructs Harry carefully — 'Yeh climb up there, jus' behind the wing joint... mind yeh don' pull any of his feathers out' — before slapping Buckbeak's hindquarters. Harry actively puts his foot on the wing and hoists himself up. Hagrid is a hands-on but instructive teacher.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Hagrid physically lifts Harry and drops him onto Buckbeak's back himself, then slaps the hindquarters before Harry is even settled. The active agency of Harry mounting the hippogriff is taken over by Hagrid, and the instructional care is reduced to physical manhandling.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Harry is an active participant who follows Hagrid's careful instruction. The film reduces Harry's agency and makes Hagrid look reckless rather than enthusiastically encouraging. It mildly shifts Hagrid from experienced-but-unorthodox teacher to careless handler.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock) — Hagrid asks 'How'm I doin' me firs' day?' after Harry's successful ride
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 19-21, 25, 43-73: Hagrid is nervously proud but never seeks validation from a student mid-lesson. His uncertainty is shown through losing his thread after Malfoy mocks him (Scene 43), but he does not directly solicit reassurance from Harry during the successful part of the lesson.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Hagrid whispers to Harry 'How'm I doin' me firs' day?' mid-lesson, explicitly seeking a student's approval of his teaching performance.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This makes Hagrid seem more insecure and self-conscious in a played-for-lightness way that undercuts the book's portrayal of him as someone who loses confidence only after real setbacks (Malfoy's injury, the governors' complaint). The book earns his vulnerability; the film inserts it as a comic beat at an inappropriate moment, flattening the arc of his confidence collapse.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock) — Only one hippogriff (Buckbeak) is shown; Hagrid brings it out of the forest alone
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 47-49: Hagrid comes jogging into the paddock holding chains attached to a dozen hippogriffs simultaneously — 'Each of the beasts had a thick leather collar around its neck, which was attached to a long chain, and the ends of all of these were held in the vast hands of Hagrid.' This display of physical strength and organisational command is a key beat of his introduction as teacher.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: A single hippogriff (Buckbeak) emerges from the trees and Hagrid simply shoos it forward. The spectacle of Hagrid managing twelve creatures at once is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's image of Hagrid commanding a dozen hippogriffs establishes him as formidably capable with magical creatures in a way the film omits. It is a minor loss but it does reduce the impression of his genuine expertise and physical command in his first lesson.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock) — Hagrid's lesson instructions are condensed; the full etiquette explanation is cut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 52-53: Hagrid delivers a clear, structured explanation: hippogriffs are proud, easily offended, never insult one, always wait for the hippogriff to make the first move, bow and wait, if it bows back you may touch it, if it doesn't — get away sharpish. This shows Hagrid as genuinely knowledgeable and instructionally competent even if unconventional.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Hagrid gives a compressed version — 'they're proud, easily offended, don't never insult one' and a brief description of the bowing protocol — but the full safety guidance and the clear cause-effect logic are truncated. He tells Harry 'let him make the firs' move... jus' take a step forward, give him a bow' with less elaboration.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor damage: the film retains the essence but loses some of the detail that demonstrates Hagrid's genuine pedagogical competence. Slightly reduces the sense that his teaching failure is due to circumstance (Malfoy), not incompetence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock) — Hagrid's reaction after Malfoy is injured: 'Class dismissed!'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 77-80: After Buckbeak slashes Malfoy, Hagrid immediately wrestles Buckbeak back into his collar, assesses the wound ('gone very white'), and Hermione runs to open the gate. Hagrid lifts Malfoy and runs with him up the slope toward the castle. The scene shows Hagrid acting swiftly and practically in a crisis, albeit shaken.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Hagrid says 'No. I'm the teacher. You all just... Class dismissed!' then swoops up Malfoy and lumbers toward the castle. The 'Class dismissed!' line is dismissive and slightly comic in register. Hermione offers to accompany him and he refuses with this line.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'Class dismissed!' delivery plays as a mild comic beat at a moment of genuine crisis. In the book Hagrid is urgently focused on Malfoy's welfare and panicked about the consequences; the film's line makes him sound more like he's brushing off the class than genuinely alarmed. It softens the gravity of the moment and slightly misrepresents his emotional register under pressure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Great Hall) — Harry says 'At least Hagrid didn't get sacked' as a mild relief
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 88-115: After the incident, Hagrid is not at dinner, then is found drunk and despairing ('Don' reckon they've ever had a teacher who lasted on'y a day before'), certain he will be fired, sobbing over the tankard. Harry and friends spend a full evening visit consoling him. The aftermath is emotionally substantial.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces the entire hut-visit-after-the-lesson scene with a single throwaway line by Harry at dinner — 'At least Hagrid didn't get sacked' — and moves directly to Sirius Black news. The full scene of Hagrid's despair, drunkenness, and the trio's loyalty visit is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is one of the most important relationship beats of the year: it shows the depth of Harry, Ron, and Hermione's loyalty to Hagrid, Hagrid's vulnerability and shame, his sobriety being enforced by Hermione, and his fierce protective anger at them being out after dark ('I'M NOT WORTH THAT!'). Its complete omission damages the emotional foundation of the Harry-Hagrid relationship and removes characterisation of Hagrid as both vulnerable and fiercely protective.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scenes 9-10 (Black Lake) — Hagrid receives the trio at the Black Lake after the hearing, skimming stones
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 167-209: Hagrid receives news of the appeal loss while at his hut, in a state of collapse — red-eyed, sobbing uncontrollably, flinging himself onto Harry's neck. The trio visits him at Christmas in the snow. The emotional register is grief, not stoic sadness. The hut visit is a prolonged scene of comfort, planning, and Hagrid revealing his Azkaban trauma.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film conflates multiple book scenes into one outdoor meeting at the Black Lake, where Hagrid skims stones and speaks with controlled sadness. He reports the outcome plainly: 'Buckbeak's bin sentenced ter death.' While red-eyed, he is composed and functional rather than overwhelmed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film loses Hagrid's raw grief and the extended scene of his Azkaban trauma revelation ('Yeh can' really remember who yeh are after a while... I used ter hope I'd jus' die in me sleep'). This is significant characterisation that deepens Hagrid beyond the gentle giant and gives him a genuine tragic dimension. The film's composed-by-the-lake version is functional but emotionally thinner.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scenes 9-10 — Hagrid's Azkaban trauma monologue is entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 200-208: Hagrid describes Azkaban in detail — reliving his expulsion from Hogwarts, his father's death, letting Norbert go; losing sense of self; hoping to die in his sleep; the dementors not caring about guilt. He also reveals his terror of returning and his consideration of letting Buckbeak go free, weighing it against fear of breaking the law. This is among the most psychologically rich material Hagrid is given in the entire series.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Azkaban monologue does not appear anywhere in the film corpus. The film Hagrid never discusses what Azkaban was like, never reveals the dementor effect on him personally, and never shows this dimension of his trauma.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging omission in the corpus. The Azkaban trauma passage is the deepest interiority Hagrid receives in Prisoner of Azkaban. It connects the dementor threat (the book's central atmospheric horror) directly to Hagrid's personal history, makes the dementors viscerally real through a character the audience loves, and gives Hagrid genuine psychological depth. Its loss reduces Hagrid to a simpler figure and severs a thematic link between his arc and the book's central horror.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 (Hagrid's hut before execution) — Hagrid facilitates Harry-Ron reconciliation and Ron-Hermione hug
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 278-310: In the hut before the execution, Hagrid is barely functional — trembling, spilling milk, staring around helplessly ('This helplessness was worse to watch than tears'). He is focused entirely on Buckbeak and on getting the children safely away. He does not manage interpersonal disputes among the trio; that is not his role in this scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Hagrid orchestrates a Harry-Ron handshake and a Ron-Hermione hug, playing an active mediating role in the trio's friendship disputes even as Buckbeak faces imminent execution. The scene has a comic register ('Crikey, tha's jus' abou' the most pathetic hug I e'er seen').
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a significant tonal misfire. The book's Hagrid in this scene is paralysed by grief and fear, barely able to make tea. Having him play warm comic mediator in a 'group hug' scene fundamentally misrepresents his emotional state at one of the most harrowing moments of his life. It also transfers to Hagrid a relationship-resolution function that the book assigns to the natural development of the trio's friendship, giving him agency he didn't have while stripping him of the grief he did have.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 (Hagrid's hut) — Hagrid's farewell before execution is managed and calm
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 278-310: Hagrid's hands tremble so badly the milk jug slips and shatters; he looks 'like a man who did not know where he was or what to do'; he spills milk all over the table; his eyes dart around looking for shreds of hope. He begs the children to leave for their own safety with fierce urgency ('Go! It's bad enough without you lot in trouble an' all!'). He then says quietly to Buckbeak 'It's okay, Beaky... it's okay...' in a heartbreaking farewell.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film version of this scene (Scene 13) shows Hagrid as scared but managing — directing Ron and Harry to shake hands, making tea, handling the discovery of Scabbers with mild exasperation. The physical breakdown detail (shattered milk jug, trembling hands) is replaced by the stone-throwing moment. His farewell to Buckbeak is not the sustained tender goodbye of the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Hagrid in this scene is among his most emotionally raw and human. The film replaces sustained grief-trembling with plot mechanics (Scabbers found, Hermione throws stones). Some emotional detail is preserved but the depth of his physical collapse under fear is lost, reducing the impact of his characterisation at a climactic moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (Three Broomsticks) — Hagrid's role in the overheard conversation is reduced; his emotional outbursts about Sirius Black are absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 127-156: Hagrid is a major voice in the Three Broomsticks conversation. He calls Black a 'Filthy, stinkin' turncoat!' loudly enough to silence half the bar; he tells the story of rescuing baby Harry from the ruins and being comforted by Black; he roars 'I COMFORTED THE MURDERIN' TRAITOR!'; and he says he'd have ripped Black limb from limb. This is Hagrid at his most emotionally volatile and revealing, connecting him directly to the Potter family history.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, the Three Broomsticks scene (Film Scene 8) shows Fudge, McGonagall, and Rosmerta discussing Sirius Black, but Hagrid's lines from this scene — his outbursts, his story of rescuing Harry, his personal grief and rage — do not appear in the film corpus excerpt. Hagrid is shown entering with Fudge (he rips the door off), but his speaking role in the conversation is not present in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Three Broomsticks scene is crucial for Hagrid-Harry relationship context: it is where Harry learns (via Hagrid's voice) the story of the night his parents died and that Hagrid was the one who carried him from the ruins. Hagrid's personal grief about Black and his connection to the Potter family tragedy deepens the emotional stakes. If this material is absent from the film, Harry loses a key Hagrid-mediated window into his own history, and Hagrid loses one of his most dramatically important scenes.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid run over by Beauxbatons carriage on arrival
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Hagrid as fully competent gamekeeper managing the arrival logistics with authority; he guides first years across the lake and is described as capable of handling even giant horses (Dumbledore assures Madame Maxime 'Hagrid is more than capable'). He is a large, imposing but reliable presence.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Hagrid being run over by the Beauxbatons carriage while holding runway signs, playing his arrival for slapstick comedy and physical incompetence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Reducing Hagrid to a figure of physical comedy at the moment he is supposed to be demonstrating his competence as gamekeeper undercuts the book's consistent portrayal of him as capable and authoritative in his domain, even if warmly eccentric. It sets a diminished tone for his character early in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Dragon-viewing scene: Hagrid's characterization of dragons
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid shows Harry the dragons secretly and with genuine reverence ('Is'n' it beautiful?'). His awe is conveyed through near-wordless wonder and his longing gaze at the Horntail and the eggs. He is the one who arranges this with purpose, showing Harry what he needs to know as an act of protective love. His love of dangerous creatures is presented as a sincere personality trait with depth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, Hagrid says 'These are seriously misunderstood creatures' and 'I have to admit that Horntail is a right nasty piece of work. Poor Ron nearly fainted just seeing him, you know.' He reveals Ron was also shown the dragons, framing the tip-off as casual and broader than the intimate, purposeful act in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's dragon-viewing scene is intimate and charged with Hagrid's protective love for Harry and his reverent awe for the creatures. The film's version reduces it to breezy exposition, losing the emotional weight of Hagrid's selfless act and his near-spiritual connection to dangerous magical creatures. The revelation that Ron was also shown them cheapens the special nature of Hagrid's gesture toward Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid's Yule Ball dance with Madame Maxime: hand on her backside
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book portrays Hagrid's courtship of Madame Maxime with touching earnestness and vulnerability. He dresses up, uses cologne, combs his hair, and later opens up about his mother and his painful childhood. His feelings are genuine and deeply felt. At the ball he waltzes with her and the relationship is handled with dignity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Hagrid letting his hand slip down to Madame Maxime's backside while dancing, played as a crude joke, with her pushing his hand back up.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This moment reduces Hagrid's sincere, tender courtship to a crude physical gag. The book invests significant effort in making Hagrid's vulnerability and romantic feeling affecting and sympathetic. The film's choice undermines both the relationship dynamic and Hagrid's dignity at the precise moment meant to show his emotional depth. It damages the audience's ability to take his romantic arc seriously.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid's backstory monologue delivered to Madame Maxime during dragon walk
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid's revelation about his mother and father is overheard by Harry during the private Yule Ball garden scene. It is deeply private, emotionally raw, and Harry notes he has 'never heard Hagrid talk about his childhood before.' The moment establishes Hagrid's half-giant heritage as a source of genuine pain and shame before it becomes a plot point. Hagrid's voice breaks when speaking of his father.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, Hagrid delivers his backstory ('l take after my mum... She left when l was about 3... my dad... died just when l started school') during the walk to see the dragons, in a comparatively casual conversational register, without the private emotional context of the garden scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Moving and flattening this disclosure strips it of its emotional power. In the book the backstory revelation is a defining character moment of vulnerability and grief. Delivered casually en route to a dragon enclosure, it loses the intimacy and weight that makes Hagrid's subsequent breakdown over the Skeeter article emotionally coherent. It also removes Harry's position as accidental, pained eavesdropper, which deepens his empathy for Hagrid.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid's response to Karkaroff's insult to Dumbledore: slamming him against a tree
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Hagrid seize Karkaroff and slam him against a tree in a fierce, spontaneous defense of Dumbledore's honor ('Apologize!'). Dumbledore immediately shouts 'Hagrid, no!' and Hagrid releases him at once, showing he is controllable even in anger. This beat demonstrates Hagrid's fierce loyalty and his physical power, but also his respect for authority.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is absent from the film corpus entirely. The corpus shows Hagrid arriving in response to Dumbledore's signal and then being sent to fetch Karkaroff, but the confrontation where Hagrid slams Karkaroff against the tree does not appear in the provided film material.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This moment is one of the most vivid demonstrations of Hagrid's loyal, protective nature toward Dumbledore. Its absence removes a key beat that shows Hagrid acting on principle with physical courage and emotional force, while also demonstrating his deference to Dumbledore's authority. It is a scene that encapsulates his character's dual nature: fierce protector and loyal subordinate.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Post-first-task: Hagrid's emotional support and confidence in Harry ('Yeh did it, Harry!')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Hagrid greeting Harry after the first task with 'Yeh did it, Harry! Yeh did it! An' agains' the Horntail an' all' - an outpouring of relief and pride that has been building since Hagrid secretly showed Harry the dragons out of protective love. This completes an emotional arc from secret warning to joyful vindication.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus does not show this post-task reunion between Harry and Hagrid at the arena. The corpus shows Harry receiving the golden egg and reuniting with Ron, but Hagrid's specific emotional greeting is absent from the film material provided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The absence of Hagrid's emotional post-task reunion with Harry breaks a small but meaningful arc: Hagrid took a risk to help Harry survive, and his relief and pride when Harry succeeds is the payoff of that sacrifice. Without it, the protective, emotionally invested dimension of their friendship is less visible in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid's toast at the outdoor gathering ('Soon to be the youngest Triwizard champion there's ever been!')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Hagrid's belief in Harry as warm, private encouragement expressed in increasingly emotional one-on-one exchanges - he claps a massive hand on Harry's shoulder, tells him he can do anything, and Harry feels unable to wipe the 'happy, confident smile off Hagrid's face.' Hagrid's faith in Harry is shown as something Harry both treasures and feels guilty about deceiving.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Hagrid toasting Harry publicly at an outdoor gathering: 'Soon to be the youngest Triwizard champion there's ever been! Hooray!' This is a public, boisterous declaration rather than the intimate, emotionally complex private encouragement of the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of Hagrid's belief in Harry carries emotional weight precisely because it is private and because Harry must hold back the truth, creating guilt and tenderness. Making it a public toast simplifies the dynamic and removes the nuanced emotional complexity of Harry's relationship with Hagrid's faith in him. It reduces a character beat to cheerleading.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid's warning to Harry about Krum and foreigners ('The less you lot 'ave ter do with these foreigners, the happier yeh'll be')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book includes this scene where Hagrid, angered by Madame Maxime's rejection, tells Harry the foreigners can't be trusted and snaps when Harry mentions Madame Maxime. Harry is glad to say goodbye to him. This is presented as a rare moment of Hagrid being wrong and emotionally compromised - a nuanced character flaw that makes him more human.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is entirely absent from the film corpus. There is no equivalent moment where Hagrid's hurt over Madame Maxime causes him to express xenophobic bitterness, nor any scene showing him being emotionally compromised after their relationship ruptures.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's willingness to show Hagrid as flawed - capable of prejudice when wounded - is part of what makes him a three-dimensional character rather than a purely benign figure. Its absence from the film removes a moment of honest character complexity and also the relational arc of Hagrid's hurt following the Madame Maxime garden scene rupture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Entire Rita Skeeter article aftermath: Hagrid hiding in his cabin, Hermione rallying him, Dumbledore's visit
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes substantial material to Hagrid's breakdown after the Skeeter article - refusing to answer the door for days, red eyes, tangled hair - and to Harry, Ron, and Hermione's determined efforts to reach him, Hermione's passionate speech outside his door, and Dumbledore's quiet, firm restoration of Hagrid's dignity with references to parent letters, his own brother, and a refusal to accept resignation. Hagrid's recovery includes him sharing the photograph of his father and making the connection between his own history and Harry's. This arc is central to Hagrid's emotional depth in the book.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire arc - the Skeeter article about Hagrid's half-giant heritage, his withdrawal, the friends' attempts to reach him, Dumbledore's intervention, and the recovery scene - is absent from the film corpus. None of this material appears in any film scene provided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most significant single loss in the adaptation. The Skeeter article arc is Hagrid's primary emotional storyline in Goblet of Fire. It develops his vulnerability, his self-doubt about his identity as a half-giant, his relationship with Dumbledore as a protector and restorer of dignity, and his parallel with Harry as an outsider. It also contains the photograph of his father - the most intimate glimpse into his backstory in the entire saga. Its complete absence means the film Hagrid has no emotional arc whatsoever in this installment, reducing him to a purely functional supporting role.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Loss of Blast-Ended Skrewts extended storyline and Hagrid's pedagogical character
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes a rich, running portrait of Hagrid as a teacher through the Skrewts: his enthusiastic incompetence, his inability to answer what they're for, his genuine delight in dangerous creatures, his telling off of Malfoy ('I hear yeh made a good ferret'), his comfort with students in his cabin over tea, darning socks, and debating house-elf rights. All this builds a vivid picture of Hagrid's pedagogical voice, his relationship with the trio, and his eccentric warmth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no Blast-Ended Skrewt lessons, no cabin visits over tea, no house-elf debate, no Hagrid-Malfoy confrontations in class, and no extended scenes of Hagrid teaching. His role as Care of Magical Creatures teacher is essentially invisible in the film beyond brief references.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Skrewt lessons collectively constitute the primary venue in which Hagrid's teaching personality, his relationship with the trio, and his characteristic mix of enthusiasm and obliviousness are displayed across the book. Their absence means the film entirely loses Hagrid as a teacher figure with a voice, a classroom presence, and an ongoing relationship with students - collapsing him into a plot-functional character without ongoing personality expression.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Hagrid's return and Umbridge interrogation at the hut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Hagrid's return as a rich, extended scene: he is battered and bleeding, reluctantly tells the story of the giant mission over tea, demonstrates warmth, stubbornness, courage, humor (beard twitching, the dragon steak comedy), and loyalty to Dumbledore. The scene runs for many pages and is a major character showcase. He also cleverly deflects Umbridge when she arrives, showing low cunning and protectiveness of Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses Hagrid's return into a brief hut scene. The giants mission is summarized in a few lines ('I tried to convince them to join the cause'), stripping out the entire narrative of Karkus, Golgomath, the Death Eaters visiting, the cave negotiations, and Olympe's role. The rich storytelling voice and the comedy of the dragon steak are entirely absent. Hagrid delivers exposition but loses the texture of character that the book scene provides.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's 'Hagrid's Tale' chapter is one of the defining Hagrid scenes of the entire saga, showcasing his courage, loyalty, warmth, humor, and stubbornness all at once. Reducing it to a functional exposition dump strips away the voice and personality that make him compelling. The audience loses the sense of what Hagrid actually endured and why it matters.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Hagrid's mission summary collapses Olympe's role and Hagrid's agency
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Hagrid as an active agent on a dangerous diplomatic mission. He navigates giant politics, assesses the Gurg, executes Dumbledore's gift strategy, perseveres after Karkus is killed, is attacked and saved by Olympe's spellwork, and independently decides to visit the resistant giants in caves. He repeatedly resists the temptation to give up ('Dumbledore was relyin' on us!'). His tenacity and moral seriousness are fully on display.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reduces the entire mission to Hagrid saying he tried to convince the giants and that Death Eaters were also trying. There is no depiction of his initiative, his persistence after Golgomath takes over, his care in following Dumbledore's instructions, or his refusal to abandon the mission. The film Hagrid simply reports failure passively.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the giant mission to show Hagrid as genuinely brave and capable, not just a lovable bumbler. He acts with strategic patience, physical courage, and moral commitment. The film's omission means the audience only ever sees Hagrid as a victim of the mission (injured, failed) rather than as someone who fought hard and intelligently for a cause. This damages his standing as a meaningful agent in the Order of the Phoenix.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Grawp introduction scene compresses and softens Hagrid's delusional stubbornness
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Hagrid as genuinely, comically self-deceived about Grawp. He brushes off Hermione's warnings, wakes Grawp up over her objections, nearly gets knocked cold himself, and ends the scene still insisting 'the attempt's comin' on fine.' His stubborn refusal to admit the obvious danger is a defining character flaw played with tragicomic tone. Firenze's warning ('his attempt is not working, he would do better to abandon it') and Harry's private despair at the situation are also present.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Grawp scene is more slapstick and lighter. Hagrid's stubbornness is present but the deeper self-delusion and the genuine distress Hermione and Harry feel about being bound to an impossible promise are muted. The film moves through the scene quickly and ends on a relatively soft comedic note (Hermione commanding Grawp and succeeding) rather than the book's tone of dread and resigned obligation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The tragicomic dimension of Hagrid's blind spot — his inability to see that his love for creatures consistently puts others at risk — is one of the book's honest character observations. Softening it into broader comedy loses the nuance that makes him a fully rounded character rather than simply a gentle giant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Umbridge's inspection of Hagrid's class is absent from film corpus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains an extended, damaging inspection sequence in which Umbridge deliberately speaks to Hagrid as though he cannot understand normal English, mimes actions at him, and solicits Pansy Parkinson's cruel assessment that his speech sounds like grunting. Hagrid flushes and struggles to maintain composure while continuing to teach. His dignity under sustained humiliation, and Hermione's furious loyalty to him, are both on full display.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus does not contain this inspection scene. Umbridge's interrogation of Hagrid at his hut is present, but the public classroom humiliation — with Hagrid trying to teach while being systematically degraded in front of students — does not appear in the provided film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The inspection scene establishes the specific nature of the prejudice Hagrid faces (his half-giant status used to paint him as sub-human and inarticulate) and shows his quiet dignity under genuine cruelty. Without it, the film's portrayal of Umbridge's campaign against Hagrid loses its most specific and pointed expression. It also removes Hermione's fierce public loyalty to him, which is important to their relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Hagrid's emotional scene in the Three Broomsticks is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains a scene where Harry finds Hagrid alone and mournful at the Three Broomsticks, fresh-cut and bruised, speaking about orphanhood, blood, and shared outsider status with Harry. He refuses to explain his injuries, is clearly suffering, and lumbers out leaving Harry worried. The scene deepens their bond and shows Hagrid's private grief and stubbornness about accepting help.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the provided film corpus. Hagrid's private emotional life outside of functional plot scenes is not represented.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Three Broomsticks scene is one of the few moments in the saga where Hagrid and Harry connect as emotional equals, both orphans navigating a hostile world. Its absence means the film's Hagrid-Harry relationship remains functional rather than deeply personal, reducing the emotional cost of Hagrid's later expulsion from Hogwarts.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Firenze's warning to Harry about Hagrid's 'attempt' is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Firenze privately warn Harry that Hagrid's attempt (to tame Grawp) is not working and he should abandon it, and that he is doing this as a service to Hagrid who saved him. This connects multiple threads: Hagrid's loyalty to Firenze, Firenze's concern for Hagrid, and the growing impossibility of the Grawp situation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus does not contain this exchange. Firenze appears but the specific warning about Hagrid and the reciprocal loyalty dynamic between Hagrid and Firenze is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Firenze-Hagrid loyalty thread enriches both characters and adds thematic depth about loyalty, protection, and the cost of caring. Its absence is a minor but real loss of relational texture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Hagrid's expulsion/fight scene is compressed and McGonagall's intervention context is reduced
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book presents Hagrid's expulsion fight as witnessed from the Astronomy Tower during the OWL exam, with Harry, Ron and Hermione watching in mounting horror. Hagrid roars defiance ('RUDDY COWARDS!'), fights off multiple Stunners due to his giant blood, carries Fang, and escapes into the night. McGonagall is Stunned defending him. The scene carries enormous emotional weight as another pillar of Hogwarts safety falls.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus describes this scene occurring but the corpus text for the film is limited here. The scene exists in the film but the book's specific emotional architecture — the exam context, the students watching helplessly, the specific beats of Hagrid's defiance — cannot be fully confirmed as present from the corpus alone. The corpus references it only briefly in the action description.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The context of the exam — students forced to keep working while watching Hagrid be attacked — is part of what makes the scene devastating in the book. If this framing is reduced in the film, the emotional impact of Hagrid's departure is correspondingly diminished. Confidence is medium given corpus limitations.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP - Hogsmeade/outside scene: Hagrid emerges from trees with stinksap bag
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid's distress over Aragog's illness is revealed in an intimate, emotionally charged visit to his cabin, where Harry, Ron, and Hermione make a deliberate effort to reconnect after weeks of estrangement. The scene includes Hagrid sulking, the trio's guilt, a confrontation at his door, and a long emotional conversation that deepens the friendship and establishes Aragog's significance gradually.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reduces Hagrid's grief over Aragog to a brief, almost comic street encounter in Hogsmeade. Hagrid pops out of trees holding a burlap bag of stinksap, cheerfully announces Aragog is ill, crosses his fingers hopefully, and disappears back into the woods. The sustained emotional arc of Hagrid's withdrawal, the trio's guilt, and the reconciliation scene is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's extended cabin visit is one of the richest Hagrid scenes in HBP: it shows his vulnerability, the trio's loyalty being tested by guilt, and establishes the emotional weight of Aragog's death that pays off later. The film's breezy substitute strips this to a throwaway gag, losing the relationship texture and the build-up that gives the funeral scene its resonance.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP - Hagrid's cabin visit: confrontation at the door and reconciliation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Hagrid giving them the cold shoulder for weeks, then slamming his door on them when they visit. Harry threatens to blast the door open, Hagrid roars 'I'm a teacher, Potter!', and the exchange of 'sir'/'Potter' leads to a grudging but warm reconciliation. This scene demonstrates Harry's assertiveness and affection, Hagrid's pride and hurt feelings, and the depth of their friendship.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire scene — the weeks of estrangement, the slammed door, the 'I'm a teacher, Potter!' confrontation, and the reconciliation — does not appear in the film corpus. The only cabin visit in the film corpus is the Aragog burial sequence, where Hagrid is already present and welcoming.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The door confrontation is one of the sharpest and most characterful exchanges Hagrid has in the entire series: it shows his dignity, his emotional fragility, and the genuine two-way nature of his friendship with Harry. Its absence removes a key moment of relationship depth and reduces Hagrid to a passive, always-available figure rather than a person with wounded pride who must be won over.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP - Hagrid's cabin: Aragog burial and indoor drinking scene (composite)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry arrives alone under the Invisibility Cloak, and Slughorn is brought in as Harry's social engineering move under Felix Felicis. Hagrid is unaware of the manipulation; he is genuinely moved by Slughorn's apparent sympathy. The scene involves extended dialogue about Aragog's history, Hagrid's personal grief, toasts, singing, Hagrid weeping about Harry's dead parents, and Hagrid eventually falling asleep while Harry extracts the memory. Crucially, Hagrid's emotional state — grief, gratitude, gentle obliviousness to being used — is rendered with great warmth and complexity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses and partially restructures the scene. The encounter with Slughorn happens outside before reaching Hagrid's cabin rather than through Harry's careful orchestration inside. The extended indoor drinking, the toasts, the singing of Odo the Hero, Hagrid's tears about Harry's parents, and Hagrid falling asleep while Harry manoeuvres Slughorn are retained in outline but the film corpus shows the scene is condensed. The emotional intimacy of Hagrid's grief speech about Harry's parents ('Bes' wiz and witchard o' their age') is present but the surrounding texture is reduced.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is a masterclass in using Hagrid's emotional openness and innocence as the unwitting vehicle for Harry's mission. The film retains the skeleton but the compression reduces Hagrid's role from emotionally complex pivot of the scene to a grieving backdrop. The loss of the extended indoor build-up slightly diminishes the portrayal of Hagrid's trusting, big-hearted nature being quietly exploited by the people who love him.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP - Katie Bell cursing scene on the road outside Hogsmeade
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry runs toward the school for help and physically collides with Hagrid coming the other way from visiting Grawp. Hagrid takes command, scoops up Katie, and sprints to the castle — a moment that shows his instinctive protectiveness and physical heroism. Harry's role is to fetch help; Hagrid arrives as the rescuer.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Hagrid lurching out of the white snow as a 'massive figure' who scoops up Katie and — in a notable addition — whispers 'Now, now. Now, now...' soothingly, like calming a terrified animal, until Katie's body goes limp. This is a film-invented action not present in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The whispering-to-calm-a-cursed-person moment is a small invention that, while not deeply damaging, slightly reframes Hagrid's instinct as mystical/animalistic rather than simply powerful and protective as in the book. It is a minor tone shift but worth noting as a divergence. The damage is low given it does not contradict his character fundamentally, merely inflects it differently.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP - Post-battle scene: Hagrid at Dumbledore's body and in castle aftermath
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid physically carries Dumbledore's body from the tower base and manages the immediate aftermath — telling McGonagall, shepherding students, being consulted by McGonagall in her office about whether Hogwarts should stay open. He gives the deeply felt line 'It's me home, it's bin me home since I was thirteen.' He also defends Dumbledore's right to be buried at Hogwarts: 'No other headmaster or headmistress ever gave more to this school.' These actions give Hagrid meaningful agency and voice in the institutional crisis.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Hagrid stopping short and being 'shattered' at the sight of Dumbledore's body, while Harry kneels beside Dumbledore, straightens his spectacles, and grieves. McGonagall leads the wand-raising tribute. The post-battle institutional scenes (McGonagall's office debate, Hagrid's views on Hogwarts staying open, his tribute to Dumbledore) are absent from the film corpus entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Hagrid is not merely a grieving witness — he performs concrete actions (moving the body, managing the crisis) and is given a formal voice in the school's future. His statements in McGonagall's office reveal how deeply Hogwarts is his identity and how personally he feels Dumbledore's loss as an institutional as well as personal tragedy. The film reduces him to a bystander at the body scene, transferring all meaningful agency and emotional statement to Harry, McGonagall, and others. This is a significant loss of Hagrid's function and dignity in the climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP - Film scene 9 (134): Hagrid's hut on fire / Snape confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid emerges from his cabin when he hears Death Eaters coming, actively fights the blond Death Eater using his natural near-invulnerability, yells about Fang being trapped, and after the battle helps Harry extinguish the fire using 'Aguamenti' from his pink umbrella. He then helps Harry up, checks on him, and the two have the devastating exchange where Harry reveals Dumbledore is dead. Hagrid refuses to believe it, confidently asserting Snape must have been keeping his cover — a characteristically loyal and tragic misreading.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Hagrid stumbling out of the burning hut after Harry's fight with Snape is already over. Hagrid says 'Take more'n tha' ter finish me off' and references Dumbledore being able to put the hut right, then expresses confusion about Snape. Critically, the film omits: Hagrid actively fighting the Death Eater during the battle, the 'Aguamenti' exchange, and the extended dialogue where Hagrid refuses to believe Dumbledore is dead and constructs an alternative explanation ('Dumbledore musta told Snape ter go with them'). Instead, Hagrid simply asks 'Where's Dumbledore?' and goes still when Harry cannot answer.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of this scene is rich with Hagrid's character: his physical courage in fighting the Death Eater, his practical co-operation with Harry to douse the flames, and above all his heartbreaking refusal to accept that Dumbledore could be dead — loyalty expressed as denial. The film skips the active fighting (reducing him from combatant to survivor) and collapses the emotional exchange to a single mute moment. The loss of Hagrid's rationalisation ('Dumbledore musta told Snape ter go with them') removes a deeply characteristic beat: his instinct to protect Dumbledore's reputation even when confronted with impossible news.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP - Ron in hospital wing: Hagrid's visit and conversation about the attacks
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid rushes to the hospital wing, mud-flecked, having been in the forest with Aragog. He is visibly distressed about Ron, speculates about a Quidditch connection, then in the corridor reveals (accidentally) that Dumbledore is angry with Snape, and stands up to Filch. The corridor scene is a substantial piece of characterisation: Hagrid as a conduit of crucial plot information, as a figure who fiercely protects the students from Filch, and as someone whose loyalty to Dumbledore makes him a poor keeper of secrets.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This hospital visit and corridor scene — including Hagrid's slip about Dumbledore and Snape's argument, the standoff with Filch, and the 'I'm a ruddy teacher' confrontation — does not appear in the film corpus at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene does triple duty in the book: it advances the Snape subplot through Hagrid's accidental disclosure, it characterises Hagrid as instinctively protective of students even in minor bureaucratic conflicts, and it shows his complex loyalty (to Dumbledore, to Harry, to his own big mouth). Its absence removes Hagrid as an active plot participant and leaves him with no function in the film's middle section beyond the Aragog subplot.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Privet Drive departure: Hagrid's greeting and transition to briefing
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid arrives as part of a group, is described physically dominating the scene ('hunchbacked to avoid hitting his head on the ceiling'), participates in the plan discussion, physically lifts Mundungus to position him, and his emotional weight in the gathering is felt through action and presence rather than comic relief. His line to Harry about the sidecar ('An' you're with me, Harry. That all righ'?... looking a little anxious') is tender and slightly self-deprecating.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Hagrid arrives, pulls a 'small twittering bird from his beard' as an immediate comic gag, and his dialogue is reduced to jokey deflection ('Yeah, he's ruddy gorgeous. What say we get undercover before someone murders him'). The book's anxious, tender check-in with Harry about the sidecar arrangement is absent; instead Hagrid simply taps the sidecar and Harry drops in without the emotional beat.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The bird-in-beard gag immediately codes Hagrid as comic prop rather than loyal protector. The book's tender, slightly anxious check-in ('That all righ'?') that establishes Hagrid's emotional attentiveness to Harry is lost, replaced by a quip that positions him as comic relief at the moment the film should be emphasising his devotion.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Sitting room briefing: Hagrid's role in the plan and Mundungus placement
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid physically picks up Mundungus by the scruff of the neck and deposits him next to Fleur, an active, decisive comic-but-purposeful action that shows Hagrid participating in the logistics of the plan with physicality and authority.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does not include Hagrid performing this action. The Mundungus repositioning beat is absent from the film corpus's briefing scene, removing a small but characteristic moment of Hagrid asserting himself within the group.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor loss, but the book beat shows Hagrid as an active, capable participant in Order logistics rather than a passive bystander. Its absence marginally flattens his presence in the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4/5/6 – Sky/motorway/tunnel chase: Hagrid's role in counter-attack
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, the aerial battle is a sustained, collaborative fight between Harry and Hagrid. Hagrid deploys multiple gadgets (wall of darkness, net, dragon-fire) at specific tactical moments, bellows encouragement and instruction, physically rescues Harry from the plummeting sidecar with a 'huge hand,' and even launches himself bodily off the bike at a Death Eater. Harry simultaneously fires Stunning Spells. The sequence is long, chaotic, and shows Hagrid as a physically brave, resourceful, if limited, combatant working in concert with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses and significantly alters the chase. On the motorway and in the tunnel, Hagrid drives and uses dragon-fire, but the specific tactical exchanges (net, wall of darkness, Hagrid bodily tackling a Death Eater, Hagrid physically hoisting Harry from the falling sidecar) are not present in the film corpus. The tunnel sequence introduces a new invention (loop-the-loop around a lorry) that centres Hagrid's driving spectacle but removes his active defensive agency. Hagrid's role becomes predominantly that of driver/vehicle operator rather than co-combatant.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Hagrid as a brave, physically decisive participant in the battle — tackling a Death Eater off his broom, hoisting Harry to safety with his bare hands, deploying gadgets strategically. The film's condensed and re-choreographed chase reduces him to a driver, making Harry the sole active agent. This understates Hagrid's courage and physical heroism, which are defining character traits.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 – Pylon chase: Hedwig's death and Harry's identification
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hedwig is killed in the sidecar while caged — a passive, shocking death that Harry cannot prevent. He is grief-stricken but must continue fighting. He later explicitly refuses to blast Stan Shunpike out of his way, uses 'Expelliarmus,' and it is this characteristic mercy that identifies him to the Death Eaters as the real Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hedwig is freed by Harry before departure and swoops into the battle of her own accord, attacking a Death Eater's wand hand before being killed by a volley of wand blasts. She dies heroically rather than helplessly. A Death Eater immediately shouts 'That's him! The real one!' — but the corpus does not show Harry casting a signature mercy spell (Expelliarmus on a known victim) as the trigger for identification. The mechanism of identification is visually implied by Harry's visible reaction/presence rather than his moral choice.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of Hedwig's death underlines Harry's helplessness and grief with no heroic frame; changing it to a sacrifice softens the loss's darkness. More significantly, the book's identification mechanism — Harry's refusal to use lethal force on Stan Shunpike, his characteristic mercy — is a morally defining moment that foreshadows his broader choices. The film loses this moral beat, replacing it with a visual identification that carries no thematic weight about Harry's values.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 – Arrival at the Burrow: Hagrid's account of the ambush and transition to waiting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry and Hagrid arrive via Portkey at Ted Tonks's house, are patched up, share a poignant moment over Hedwig's death, and Hagrid greets Harry's survival with a rib-cracking hug and the line 'Blimey, Harry, how did yeh get out o' that? I thought we were both goners.' There is also a moment where Hagrid asks about Hedwig, triggering Harry's grief, and Hagrid comforts him gruffly ('Never mind. She had a great old life').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Harry and Hagrid crash-land the motorbike directly at the Burrow (skipping Ted Tonks's house entirely). The Hedwig grief moment and Hagrid's gruff comfort ('Never mind. She had a great old life') are absent. The hug is present in film Scene 9 implicitly (they arrive together) but the intimate two-person aftermath — the grief beat, Hagrid's comfort, the Tonks household — is replaced by an immediate community reunion.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's detour to Ted Tonks's house isolates Harry and Hagrid together, allowing a private moment of relief, grief over Hedwig, and Hagrid's characteristic gruff tenderness. This is one of the most intimate one-on-one scenes between them in the book. Its removal collapses their private bond into the crowd, losing relationship texture that is important given how central the Hagrid-Harry relationship is to the saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11 – Sitting room aftermath: Hagrid's response to the betrayal accusation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid asks 'So why aren' you checkin' me?' when Lupin interrogates Harry but not him, receives a logical answer (Polyjuice is for humans only), and then collapses a chair sitting down. Harry's internal thought — looking at Hagrid who risked his life, who once was tricked into giving Voldemort crucial information — is a complex, loving, bittersweet observation that holds Hagrid's flaws and virtues simultaneously. Harry's speech defending trust is specifically directed partly at Hagrid.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hagrid delivers a rambling, comic, self-exculpatory monologue ('I'd wager me life it wasn' none of you lot... Talk in me sleep on occasion... mostly it's gibberish... I'd cut me tongue out 'fore I'd betray 'arry e'en in me dreams') that makes everyone smile before Hagrid notices and asks 'Wha's so funny!' The scene plays as comic relief. The book's nuanced internal observation by Harry about Hagrid's past mistake with Norbert/Voldemort is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film converts a moment of nuanced characterisation — Hagrid as someone Harry loves and trusts despite knowing his capacity for accidental betrayal — into a straight comedy beat. The book's version is more emotionally complex: Harry's silent acknowledgment of Hagrid's past flaw, held alongside his love, is thematically rich. The film's Hagrid is simply funny here; the book's Hagrid is funny and flawed and beloved. The comedy is not wrong in itself, but it displaces depth.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 – Wedding: Hagrid's birthday interaction with Harry and gift of the mokeskin purse
